clue.text: Those amused when large queen is embraced by Ryan?

indicators.note: being embraced means being held inside, so the first letters sit within the footballer's surname

blocks.note: L is the standard abbreviation for large, as on clothing labels
ER, Elizabeth Regina, the usual crossword queen
Ryan Giggs, the Welsh footballer who played for Manchester United

explanation.surface: A footballer named Ryan hugs a queen, and onlookers are amused by the moment.
explanation.walkthrough: Ryan is not a person to define but a first name pointing to the Welsh footballer Ryan Giggs, whose surname does the embracing.
explanation.definitionFit: People who giggle are laughing nervously or with amusement, so a group of them are folk who find something funny.

clue.text: Chorister heading off after good redhead

indicators.note: with its heading off, the word loses its first letter
after places the clipped singer behind the good abbreviation

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
a chorister is a singer, minus its first letter

explanation.surface: A choirboy sets off after a well-behaved red-haired child.
explanation.definitionFit: Ginger is the British nickname for someone with red or orange hair.

clue.text: Scots go around police cell

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the Scots verb encloses the police force

blocks.note: gae is the Scots form of go
the Met is London's Metropolitan Police

explanation.surface: Scottish officers march round a police cell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Police cell' looks like a jail, but cell alone is the biological definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A gamete is a reproductive cell, an egg or sperm, that fuses with another at fertilisation.

clue.text: Laurel got mixed up with this lout

indicators.note: mixed up means jumbled, so the two words before it are scrambled together

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the letters that come out of the jumble beside the answer

explanation.surface: Stan Laurel got muddled up with a yob.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the letters of Laurel and got rearrange into this answer plus lout, giving the British phrase lager lout, a drunken hooligan.
explanation.definitionFit: This stands for the word that pairs with lout, and lager is the pale beer that names the drunken yob.

clue.text: Said to stagger with pain supping too much of this?

indicators.note: said means spoken, so the sounds of the next words matter, not their spelling

blocks.note: to reel is to stagger
to ail is to suffer pain

explanation.surface: Drinking too much leaves someone lurching and hurting.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue paints the effect: drink too much of this and you will reel and ail. Real ale is a British term for traditionally brewed cask beer.
explanation.definitionFit: This points to the beer whose overconsumption brings staggering, and real ale is cask-conditioned British beer.

clue.text: Humiliates gutless armies defending headquarters

indicators.note: without guts means the inside is removed, leaving only the first and last letters of the word
defenders surround what they protect, so the outer letters wrap around the other piece

blocks.note: the first and last letters of armies
a base is a military headquarters

explanation.surface: Hollowed-out armies protecting their headquarters suffer humiliation.
explanation.definitionFit: To abase someone is to lower or degrade them, which is what humiliating a person does.

clue.text: Swimmer well following dismal week

indicators.note: following places the healthy word after the gloomy one and the week

blocks.note: feeling blue is feeling low
W is the abbreviation for week
hale means healthy, as in hale and hearty

explanation.surface: A swimmer feels better after a miserable week.
explanation.walkthrough: Swimmer suggests a person; it is the largest animal in the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The blue whale is a huge marine mammal, and anything that lives in the sea can be called a swimmer.

clue.text: Wise man defends pressure point in the modern era

indicators.note: a defender stands around what it guards, so the wise man's letters surround the rest

blocks.note: P is the physics symbol for pressure
an ace is a winning point served in tennis
a sage is a wise person

explanation.surface: A wise elder guards a pressure point in the present day.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes the era of space exploration and advanced technology, so the present age of modernity.

clue.text: Watch supply teacher's pet avoiding her

indicators.note: avoiding means leaving out, so the pronoun at the end is taken away
supply here is an adjective meaning in a supple, flexible way, so the letters bend into a new order

blocks.note: all the letters of the phrase
removed from the phrase

explanation.surface: A cover teacher's favourite pupil keeps out of her way, merely looking on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply teacher' reads as a stand-in teacher, but supply is the anagram signal for what remains once her is removed.
explanation.definitionFit: To spectate is to look on at an event without taking part, which is to observe it.

clue.text: Mathematician's device turned on by minute unit of mass

indicators.note: turned means flipped round, so the little word that follows is read backwards

blocks.note: the little word on, taken as written before it is flipped
MO is a short moment, as in 'half a mo'
the gram is a metric unit of mass

explanation.surface: A mathematician's gadget is switched on by a tiny unit of weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned on' reads as switched on, but it is the instruction to reverse the word on.
explanation.definitionFit: A nomogram is a chart of scaled lines used to read off calculated values graphically, a calculating aid for mathematicians.

clue.text: Ruffian took in minister

blocks.note: a cur is a contemptible, low fellow
to take food in is to eat it

explanation.surface: A thug swindled a clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Took in' suggests deceiving someone, but here it means consumed.
explanation.definitionFit: A curate is an assistant member of the clergy in a parish, a type of Christian minister.

clue.text: Retreats back to dock

indicators.note: back means going backwards, so the hideaways are read from right to left

blocks.note: dens are private retreats or hideaways

explanation.surface: Ships pull back into harbour to dock.
explanation.walkthrough: Dock suggests ships; here it means to cut short, a Scots and dialect sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Sned is a dialect verb meaning to lop or prune branches, just as docking cuts off a tail.

clue.text: Think about electronic disruption of intranet

indicators.note: a disruption throws things into disorder, so the network's letters are scrambled

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for electronic, as in e-mail
an internal company network, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone ponders an electronic fault that has knocked out the office network.
explanation.definitionFit: To entertain an idea is to consider it seriously, so the verb can mean contemplate or weigh up.

clue.text: It has ears, hearing French octet?

indicators.note: hearing tells us to go by the sound of the French word rather than its spelling

blocks.note: huit is French for eight

explanation.surface: Something with ears listening to a group of eight French musicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It has ears' sounds like an animal or person with hearing; the ears are the grain heads of a cereal.
explanation.definitionFit: A cereal crop carries its grain in clusters called ears at the top of each stalk.

clue.text: Knocked over energy drink and pasty

indicators.note: something knocked over is turned upside down, which in a clue means written backwards

blocks.note: E is the physics symbol for energy
to lap is to drink as a cat does

explanation.surface: Someone spills an energy drink next to their Cornish pasty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pasty' looks like the baked pie; it is the adjective for an unhealthy pale complexion.
explanation.definitionFit: A pasty face is pallid and unhealthy looking, lacking colour.

clue.text: IT hacker with a novel punishment

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are made into a fresh arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A computer hacker is given an unusual sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: Novel reads as a book, but it signals rearranging the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A thick ear is a British idiom for a clout round the head, a swollen ear given as a physical penalty.

clue.text: Current game is curtailed

indicators.note: curtailed means having its tail cut off, so the final letter of the game goes

blocks.note: draughts is the board game called checkers in America

explanation.surface: A game in progress is cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' reads like present or ongoing, but it is a noun: a current of air.
explanation.definitionFit: A draught is a flow of cold air through a room, a current of air.

clue.text: Have dog help after unpackaging kind of shop product

indicators.note: unpackaging strips away the wrapping, leaving just the inner letters of the word

blocks.note: to own is to have
a lab is a Labrador retriever
the inner letters of help

explanation.surface: Get a dog to help after unpacking the shopping.
explanation.definitionFit: Own-label goods are sold under a supermarket's own brand, a category of store merchandise.

clue.text: Tories in good French conference venue

indicators.note: in places the party group inside the French word

blocks.note: bon is French for good
the Tories are the political right

explanation.surface: Conservatives in a fine French setting for a party gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tories are Britain's Conservative Party; BRIGHTON is the English seaside town that hosts party conferences.
explanation.definitionFit: Brighton, on England's south coast, regularly hosts political party conferences in its large seafront centre.

clue.text: Honour magistrate in service?

blocks.note: first meaning: to revere or venerate
second meaning: a magistrate is addressed as Your ___, and a church service is also called this

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: the magistrate's title and an act of church service are the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: Worship is reverent devotion, and English mayors and magistrates are formally styled His or Your Worship.

clue.text: Turned up voucher for booze

indicators.note: turned up in a down clue means flipped to read from bottom to top

blocks.note: a slip is a small piece of paper such as a voucher

explanation.surface: A voucher turned up that can be exchanged for drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: Pils is a pale Pilsner lager, one variety of alcoholic drink.

clue.text: Porter runs after busy person

indicators.note: after sends the runs abbreviation second, behind the hard-working insect

blocks.note: as busy as a bee
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A hotel porter dashes about behind a hard-working colleague.
explanation.walkthrough: Porter looks like a luggage carrier; it is a dark beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Porter is a dark brown ale brewed from roasted malt, one particular kind of the drink.

clue.text: Verbosity of dreadful abbots introducing Mass

indicators.note: dreadful means very bad, so the monks' letters are put into poor order
introducing means bringing inside, so the church service's letter goes into the jumble

blocks.note: taken letter for letter before being jumbled
M is the physics abbreviation for mass

explanation.surface: Terrible abbots pad out the Mass with long-winded talk.
explanation.walkthrough: Mass looks like the church service, but it is the scientific quantity abbreviated to M.
explanation.definitionFit: Bombast is pompous, inflated language, words that are high-sounding but empty.

clue.text: Pass pork pie for dog

blocks.note: a col is a mountain pass
pork pie is Cockney rhyming slang for lie

explanation.surface: Someone hands a pork pie to the dog.
explanation.walkthrough: Pork pie is Cockney rhyming slang: the words rhyme with lie, so a porky is an untruth.
explanation.definitionFit: A collie is a sheepdog breed from Scotland, used for herding.

clue.text: With which the start of Easter breaks Lenten disciplines

definitions.text: With which the start of Easter breaks Lenten disciplines

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter alone
breaking into something means getting inside it, so the letter goes within the disciplines

blocks.note: the first letter of Easter
fasting is the self-denial kept through Lent

explanation.surface: Easter arrives and ends the fasting of Lent with celebrations.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: E breaks FASTS, and Easter breaks Lent's fasting with celebratory meals.
explanation.definitionFit: Large celebratory meals are how Easter Sunday ends the weeks of Lenten abstinence.

clue.text: See American grunt caught in good argument?

blocks.note: lo is an old word for look or see, as in 'lo and behold'
a GI is an American soldier; grunt is US slang for an infantryman
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: An American soldier is caught up in a good argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught in' looks like a container instruction, but caught just supplies its abbreviation and 'in' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Logic is sound reasoning, the quality that makes a case convincing and valid.

clue.text: Let Simeon cast rock

indicators.note: to cast is to throw, and thrown letters land in a new order

blocks.note: the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Simeon is allowed to throw a rock.
explanation.definitionFit: Limestone is a sedimentary rock made largely of calcium carbonate.

clue.text: Overweight solicitors cycling

indicators.note: cycling means going round, so the last letter moves round to the front

blocks.note: touts solicit custom, selling tickets or trade

explanation.surface: Plump lawyers are out on their bikes.
explanation.walkthrough: Solicitors suggests lawyers; here it is people who solicit business.
explanation.definitionFit: Stout describes a heavily built, rather fat person; it is also a dark beer.

clue.text: Raw alcohol

blocks.note: first meaning: piercingly cold, as a wind
second meaning: a hoppy draught beer

explanation.walkthrough: Raw alcohol suggests neat spirits; the words are separate meanings. Bitter is a British term for a pale, hoppy ale.
explanation.definitionFit: A raw, biting wind is called bitter, and bitter is also the British name for a well-hopped ale.

clue.text: Lads come rampaging for one facing the sword?

indicators.note: rampaging means running wild, so the letters run amok into a new order

blocks.note: the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A gang of lads comes charging at someone who faces a swordsman.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks a definition by example: the courtier in the Greek legend.
explanation.definitionFit: In legend the courtier Damocles sat beneath a sword hung by a single hair, a symbol of looming peril.

clue.text: Poetry about river boats

indicators.note: about means around, so the verse word wraps round the river's letter

blocks.note: lines of verse
R is the map abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Poems written about river craft.
explanation.definitionFit: Liners are large passenger ships, so they are vessels on a grand scale.

clue.text: Paragon expresses hesitations in speech

blocks.note: ST, saint, a paragon of virtue
to utter is to say or express

explanation.surface: A model speaker voices the stammers in his delivery.
explanation.walkthrough: Expresses reads as the verb of the sentence, but it is a wordplay piece following ST.
explanation.definitionFit: Stutters are involuntary repetitions and breaks when speaking, the faltering of a stammer.
